newsitem.title: USA: Contrarians see U.S. rates down, economy cooling.
newsitem.headline: Contrarians see U.S. rates down, economy cooling.

text.p: Swimming against Wall Street's tighter credit tide, a growing minority of economists expects U.S. interest rates to remain steady or actually drop over the next 12 months.
"You can expect that minority view to become a majority view in the weeks and months ahead," said Alan Levenson, money market economist at UBS Securities Inc.Alan Greenspan's virtues.

The sentiment, bolstered by the Federal Reserve's decision to keep monetary policy unchanged earlier this week, stems from the notion that the economy is cooling without the help of further central bank action.
"We think the Federal Reserve is basically on vacation for at least until the middle of winter," said Vincent Malanga, an economist at LaSalle Economics in New York.
Several aspects of the current economic cycle, mainly in the consumer and banking sectors, support the view that the economy may slow without Fed intervention.

Financial conditions remain mostly on the restrictive side. Long-term interest rates, for example, have risen already to 6.88 percent from 6.03 percent in January, when the Fed last cut interest rates.
Thus, analysts said that a slowdown in bank loan growth, tighter lending standards and a more gradual pace of wealth creation in the equity market are all tightening financial conditions.
Also, consumer debt has swollen to post-war record levels, a phenomena that has cast a shadow on forecasts about the behavior of spending in the medium to long term.

"Consumers in the first half of the year were spending money faster than it was coming in," said Bruce Steinberg, economist and manager of macroanalysis at Merrill Lynch and Co Inc. "Job growth was strong, but they managed to spend a lot faster than even the income that was generated by that job growth," he added.
If higher debt is any indication of caution for future spending, analysts said consumers should think twice before reaching into their pockets in the months ahead.
The consumer sector accounts for around two-thirds of the nation's Gross Domestic Product.

Analysts said though that taking such an approach on the economy requires some confidence and a lot of patience. But being as it is, patience appears to be one of Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan's virtues.

"Greenspan started the second half of the year with a firm view that the economy was going to slow down early enough and fast enough to head off any inflationary pressures before they really began building," said Joseph Liro, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Inc.
"Now in September, with the August data and particularly the retail sales and the trade numbers, he's got some modest amount of hope that his forecast will come true," he added.
The lack of hard evidence that slight increases in wages seen recently will inevitably trigger inflation is another reason prompting the Fed to remain on hold, analysts said.
"The labor market is tight and wage rates are rising, but it hasn't produced any inflation yet," said Charles Lieberman, chief economist at Chase Securities Inc.
If the forecasts for slower economic growth materialize, analysts said that just about everyone, from bond investors to mortgage holders, could gain.
"More often on adjusted rates, like mortage rates on equity loans and things like that ... you would see those rates going down," Levenson said.

The UBS economist, an aggressive defender of lower rates, said he expects the Federal Reserve to cut the federal funds rate -- currently at 5.25 percent -- by 75 basis points over the balance of 1997.
"The first installment, the first 25-basis-point cut in the funds rate, will come in the first quarter," he said.
The federal funds rate is the overnight rate banks charge each other for overnight loans.
